{{short description|Shape taken by a self-gravitating fluid body rotating at constant velocity}}
[[File:Haumea Rotation.gif|thumb|right|Artistic rendering of [[Haumea]], a dwarf planet with triaxial ellipsoid shape.]]

A '''Jacobi ellipsoid''' is a [[triaxial ellipsoid|triaxial (i.e. scalene) ellipsoid]] under [[hydrostatic equilibrium]] which arises when a [[Self-gravitation|self-gravitating]], [[fluid]] body of uniform [[density]] rotates with a constant [[angular velocity]]. It is named after the German mathematician [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Jacobi |first=C. G. |year=1834 |title=Ueber die Figur des Gleichgewichts |journal=[[Annalen der Physik]] |volume=109 |issue=8–16 |pages=229–233 |doi=10.1002/andp.18341090808 |bibcode=1834AnP...109..229J |url=https://zenodo.org/record/2027349 |language=de }}</ref>

==History==
Before Jacobi, the [[Maclaurin spheroid]], which was formulated in 1742, was considered to be the only type of [[ellipsoid]] which can be in equilibrium.<ref>{{cite book |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |year=1969 |title=Ellipsoidal figures of equilibrium |volume=10 |page=253 |location=New Haven |publisher=Yale University Press }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |year=1967 |title=Ellipsoidal figures of equilibrium—an historical account |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=251–265 |doi= 10.1002/cpa.3160200203}}</ref> [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]] in 1811<ref>Lagrange, J. L. (1811). ''Mécanique Analytique'' sect. IV 2 vol.</ref> considered the possibility of a tri-axial ellipsoid being in equilibrium, but concluded that the two equatorial axes of the [[ellipsoid]] must be equal, leading back to the solution of Maclaurin spheroid. But [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi|Jacobi]] realized that [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]]'s demonstration is a sufficiency condition, but not necessary. He remarked:<ref>{{cite journal |last=Dirichlet |first=G. L. |year=1856 |title=Gedächtnisrede auf Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi |journal=[[Crelle's Journal|Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]] |volume=52 |pages=193–217 |language=de }}</ref>
<blockquote>"One would make a grave mistake if one supposed that the spheroids of revolution are the only admissible figures of equilibrium even under the restrictive assumption of second-degree surfaces" (...) "In fact a simple consideration shows that ellipsoids with three unequal axes can very well be figures of equilibrium; and that one can assume an ellipse of arbitrary shape for the equatorial section and determine the third axis (which is also the least of the three axes) and the angular velocity of rotation such that the ellipsoid is a figure of equilibrium."</blockquote>

==Jacobi formula==
[[File:Jacobi-ellipsoid-dimensions-1.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|right|The equatorial (''a'', ''b'') and polar (''c'') semi-principal axes of a Jacobi ellipsoid and Maclaurin spheroid, as a function of normalized angular momentum, subject to ''abc''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 (i.e. for constant volume of 4{{pi}}/3).<br/>The broken lines are for the Maclaurin spheroid in the range where it has dynamic but not secular stability – it will relax into the Jacobi ellipsoid provided it can dissipate energy by virtue of a viscous constituent fluid.]]

For an ellipsoid with equatorial semi-principal axes <math>a, \ b</math> and polar semi-principal axis  <math>c</math>, the angular velocity <math>\Omega</math> about <math>c</math> is given by

:<math>\frac{\Omega^2}{\pi G\rho} = 2 abc \int_0^\infty \frac{u\,du}{(a^2+u)(b^2+u)\Delta}\ , \quad \Delta^2 = (a^2+u)(b^2+u)(c^2+u),</math>

where <math>\rho</math> is the density and <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]], subject to the condition

:<math>a^2 b^2 \int_0^\infty \frac{du}{(a^2+u)(b^2+u)\Delta} = c^2\int_0^\infty \frac{du}{(c^2+u)\Delta}.</math>

For fixed values of <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>, the above condition has solution for <math>c</math> such that

:<math>\frac{1}{c^2}>\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{b^2}.</math>

The integrals can be expressed in terms of [[Elliptic integral|incomplete elliptic integral]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Darwin |first=G. H. |year=1886 |title=On Jacobi's figure of equilibrium for a rotating mass of fluid |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London |volume=41 |issue=246–250 |pages=319–336 |doi=10.1098/rspl.1886.0099 |bibcode=1886RSPS...41..319D |s2cid=121948418 |doi-access= }}</ref> In terms of the [[Carlson symmetric form]] elliptic integral <math>R_{J}</math>, the formula for the angular velocity becomes

:<math>\frac{\Omega^2}{\pi G \rho} = \frac{4 a b c}{3 (a^2 - b^2)} [a^2 R_J(a^2,b^2,c^2,a^2) - b^{2} R_J(a^2,b^2,c^2,b^2)]</math>

and the condition on the relative size of the semi-principal axes <math>a, \ b, \ c</math> is

:<math> \frac{a^2 b^2}{b^2 - a^2} [R_J(a^2,b^2,c^2,a^2) - R_J(a^2,b^2,c^2,b^2)] =  c^2 R_J(a^2,b^2,c^2,c^2).</math>

The angular momentum <math>L</math> of the Jacobi ellipsoid is given by

:<math>\frac{L}{\sqrt{GM^3 r}} = \frac{\sqrt 3}{10}\frac{a^2+b^2}{r^2}\sqrt{\frac{\Omega^2}{\pi G\rho}} \ , \quad r=\sqrt[3]{abc},</math>

where <math>M</math> is the mass of the ellipsoid and <math>r</math> is the ''mean radius'', the radius of a sphere of the same volume as the ellipsoid.

==Relationship with Dedekind ellipsoid==

The Jacobi and Dedekind ellipsoids are both equilibrium figures for a body of rotating homogeneous self-gravitating fluid. However, while the Jacobi ellipsoid spins bodily, with no internal flow of the fluid in the rotating frame, the Dedekind ellipsoid maintains a fixed orientation, with the constituent fluid circulating within it. This is a direct consequence of [[Dirichlet's ellipsoidal problem#Dedekind's theorem|Dedekind's theorem]].

For any given Jacobi ellipsoid, there exists a Dedekind ellipsoid with the same semi-principal axes <math>a, \ b, \ c</math> and same mass and with a [[flow velocity|flow velocity field]] of<ref name="Chandrasekhar1965"/>

:<math>\mathbf{u} = \zeta \frac{- a^2 y \mathbf{\hat{x}} + b^2 x \mathbf{\hat{y}}}{a^2 + b^2},</math>

where <math>x, \ y, \ z</math> are Cartesian coordinates on axes <math>\hat{x}, \ \hat{y}, \ \hat{z}</math> aligned respectively with the <math>a, \ b, \ c</math> axes of the ellipsoid. Here <math>\zeta</math> is the [[vorticity]], which is uniform throughout the spheroid (<math>\nabla\times \mathbf{u} = \zeta \mathbf{\hat{z}}</math>). The angular velocity <math>\Omega</math> of the Jacobi ellipsoid and vorticity of the corresponding Dedekind ellipsoid are related by<ref name="Chandrasekhar1965"/>

:<math>\zeta = \left( \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a}\right) \Omega.</math>

That is, each particle of the fluid of the Dedekind ellipsoid describes a [[similarity (geometry)|similar]] elliptical circuit in the same period in which the Jacobi spheroid performs one rotation.

In the special case of <math>a = b</math>, the Jacobi and Dedekind ellipsoids (and the Maclaurin spheroid) become one and the same; bodily rotation and circular flow amount to the same thing. In this case <math>\zeta = 2 \Omega</math>, as is always true for a rigidly rotating body.

In the general case, the Jacobi and Dedekind ellipsoids have the same energy,<ref name="Bardeen"/> but the angular momentum of the Jacobi spheroid is the greater by a factor of<ref name="Bardeen"/>

:<math>\frac{L_{\mathrm{Jac}}}{L_{\mathrm{Ded}}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a}\right).</math>
